content: Kernicterus is a rare neurological condition that can develop in some newborns with severe jaundice. It is also referred to as bilirubin encephalopathy. Symptoms of Kernicterus The symptoms of kernicterus vary depending on the stage of the condition: Early Stage Symptoms: Severe jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes) Absence of the startle reflex Difficulty feeding or sucking Extreme sleepiness or lethargy Mid-Stage Symptoms: High-pitched crying Arching of the back with the neck hyperextended backward Bulging of the fontanel (the soft spot on a baby’s head) Seizures Late-Stage Symptoms (Full Neurological Syndrome): High-frequency hearing loss Intellectual disability Muscle rigidity Speech difficulties Seizures Movement disorders Causes of Kernicterus Kernicterus is caused by extremely high levels of bilirubin in the blood. Bilirubin is a yellow pigment produced during the normal breakdown of old red blood cells. When bilirubin levels become excessively high, it can lead to jaundice, characterized by yellowing of the skin and eyes. In severe cases, or when the baby is critically ill, bilirubin can cross the blood-brain barrier and accumulate in brain tissue. This can result in serious neurological complications, including brain damage and hearing loss. Kernicterus typically develops within the first week of life but can occur up to the third week. Newborns with hemolytic disease of the newborn, such as Rh hemolytic disease, are at particularly high risk for severe jaundice that can lead to kernicterus. However, kernicterus has also been observed in otherwise healthy infants. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Immediate medical attention is necessary if your baby shows any signs of kernicterus. Diagnosis Kernicterus is diagnosed through a blood test that reveals elevated bilirubin levels, typically greater than 20–25 mg/dL. It is important to note that normal bilirubin ranges may vary slightly between laboratories. Discuss the specific results with your healthcare provider to understand their significance. Treatment Options Treatment for kernicterus depends on the baby’s age (in hours) and the presence of any risk factors, such as prematurity. Treatment options may include: Phototherapy (light therapy): This helps break down bilirubin in the skin. Exchange transfusions: This involves replacing the baby’s blood with donor blood to rapidly reduce bilirubin levels. Where to Find Medical Care Specialized hospitals and medical centers provide treatment for kernicterus. Seek care at facilities equipped to manage this condition. Prognosis Kernicterus is a serious condition with a guarded prognosis. Many infants with late-stage neurological complications do not survive. Possible Complications Permanent brain damage Hearing loss Death Prevention Early diagnosis and treatment of jaundice or conditions that lead to jaundice are critical in preventing kernicterus. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that: Infants showing the first signs of jaundice should have their bilirubin levels measured within 24 hours. If bilirubin levels are high, the infant should be screened for conditions involving red blood cell destruction (hemolysis). All newborns should have a follow-up appointment within 2 to 3 days after hospital discharge, especially if they are premature or near-term.
